p: Well, obviously, because you have to man the equipment.

So let's just say, throughout the day, in a school where there are

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 92 Committee on Public Safety metal detectors, you have nine to 10 agents. After the morning, uh, I want to say morning rush, but when students are actually coming into school, are those agents assigned to other schools or do they stay (INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)

No, they’re not. They stay at the school obviously, you know, aside from scanning, that's just like, what one of the duties say they do, but they are assigned to either a fixed post in schools conducting interior patrol, you know, manning the desk, greeting the visitors, doing administrative duties, obviously responding to incidents on school grounds and engaging in the escalation, preventing a lot of the violent crimes that can potentially happen on school grounds.

Thank you. So you mentioned also in your testimony that your current headcount is 3,915 agents, which is a huge drop over the last 10 years. How has that impacted the day-to-day work of a School Safety Agent? (TIMER)

Well, as I mentioned earlier, yes, we recognize that we have the vacancies, but that hasn't deviated from our mission

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 93 Committee on Public Safety of providing safety. And obviously we see that on... (CROSS-TALK)
I'm sure of that, but I'm sure it presents challenges, right? If I have 10 staff and now I have two staff, what are the challenges that they're facing daily?
I'm sorry, can you repeat your question?
Sure. Chairs, if I may?
(INAUDIBLE)

So you went from, I believe, in 2016, 4,926, so roughly 5,000 School Safety Agents. You're now at 3,915. That's a drop in staff. So given that, what challenges does that present for a School Safety Agent working in school — day-to-day challenges? Or is there no impact from the drop?

Well, obviously, they do work probably a few more hours. We have extended our dismissal coverage, obviously, to ensure the safety of our schools and of our students, as they go home as well. So, that will probably have the most impact.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 94 Committee on Public Safety
Okay, I know I'm out of time, so thank you.
Okay.
Thank you.

Thank you. I just want to point out, just to be clear, it's forced overtime that the school safety units are forced to take overtime, and then some of them, again, are getting comp time for this and taking days off. And just to repeat what you testified to, on any given day, 20% of agents can be out, resulting in multiple schools with fewer agents than they're assigned.

Chair, if you please allow me, we have a system in place, and when I said that our overtime assignments are voluntary, they are voluntary for two reasons: First of all, because of collective bargaining, we can't force School Safety Agents to work. We could request that they work up to two tours a month. So two tours a month do not amount to a large number of hours. So it is voluntary. There's a sign-up, but we have something in place; there's a sign-up sheet that every borough has, and everybody signs up for overtime as they please.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 95 Committee on Public Safety

Is the data public on how many hours of overtime each agent has or the average each agent has? Because again, what the agents are telling me, what the principals are telling me, is not what you are telling me. So I don't know where the miscommunication is. You may be talking about Level III, but the Level I agents-- tell me all the time, forced overtime, is that data public? And if not, can you share with us today?
No, it's not public.
Can you share with the Committee today?
We could circle back.
Can you-- can you...
I will be open...
Can you share with the Committee today?
I will be open to having a follow-up conversation on that.

Well, I mean, this is the conversation, right? That's why we have the hearing. I mean, I'm simply asking how many agents

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 96 Committee on Public Safety are taking overtime, and to what extent they are taking overtime? I'm sure, I'm sure that data that you have. You guys are very, very good at data and...
Chair Dinowitz, I oversee the overtime.
Great.
Looking at the overtime specifically, not operationally, but from a payroll and spending perspective.
Okay.
So in FY25, which is the last full fiscal year, on average, School Safety Agents had about 402 hours of overtime on average per School Safety Agent, which is roughly 33 hours per month on average.
Thank you. I am going to ask more about that. But I'll turn it over to Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chairs. I don't think I’ll have a chance to get to my questions, but I heard and read the testimony from Deputy Chief Mary King that yes, the authorized headcount for School Safety Agents is 3,915, and there are 316 School Safety Agent vacancies.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 97 Committee on Public Safety And do you agree that 10 years ago, in 2016, as pointed out by Councilman Hankerson, we had 5,000 School Safety Agents?
I mean, that's what the data shows, but obviously...

Okay, so the data shows that we had 5,000 School Safety Agents. So there's a big drop. We lost-- we have 1,000 fewer School Safety Agents compared to 2016. Doesn't that show that we are short of School Safety Agents, or do you have a different interpretation?

It does, but we are relentless when it comes to our recruitment efforts. And I'll expand on that. Currently have a class of-- We had a new hire class of School Safety Agents, that is currently in the Academy, expected to graduate in the next couple of weeks, of 93. Our recruitment efforts are ongoing. We have partnered up with DOE, and also our labor unions, especially the CSA, which has basically helped us to do outreach during open filing periods. We have our Community Affairs, I'm sorry, Community Outreach Unit, which is within the School Safety Division, which is also reaching out to colleges and high schools. Our NYPD Recruitment

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 98 Committee on Public Safety Section also does its own outreach, and obviously, as I mentioned in my testimony, we utilize social media to push out. So all that work that we have put into recruiting has resulted in a pool of over 1,000 Assistant School Safety Agents that are ready to be hired when the time comes. And also, there was just a School Safety test on March 23rd, of which 881 candidates passed the test. So that's the number of candidates, and when the time comes, hopefully, a list will be established. So yes, we have the vacancies. I'm not negating any of that. But are we working to make improvements? I think we are definitely moving in the right direction. There's a lot of work to do, I'm not denying that, but we are definitely moving in the right direction.

Okay, there's a graduating class of 93 School Safety Agents, but we have 360 openings, right? So you still have around 200 more that you have to hire just to fill up these openings. But again, macroscopically, we are 1,000 fewer School Safety Agents compared to 10 years ago.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 99 Committee on Public Safety And then this is how I see it, right? Mayor de Blasio wanted to dissolve the whole unit. And then, as a result of that, hundreds, if not thousands, of School Safety Agents filed for retirement and just left the job. And after that, I just don't see the effort to budget or hire back these vacancies as a result of this mass exodus. Is this something you agree with? Is that what happened, or something else happened?
I can't really answer it. I was just assigned here nine months ago. I could attest to the work that I'm doing since I got assigned to School Safety. I can't speak of what happened prior to that.

Okay, all right. What about crossing guards? Everyone is talking about School Safety Agents. It’s important, but what about the crossing guards? Is there a shortage of that, or what is the authorized headcount for that? And how many vacancies do you have? Can anyone on the panel answer that?

Good afternoon, Council Member. So school crossing guards and the

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 100 Committee on Public Safety program itself report up to my office, the Chief of Patrols Office, and it's under my purview. I'll give you a snapshot of the school crossing guards as of April 13th, 2026. Authorized head count is 2,309. Our actual head count is 2,160. That means we have a vacancy of 149. We have an additional 45 that are not accounted for in that number that are out long-term sick. We currently have 100 that we expect to hire on May 11th. So they'll be getting trained. (TIMER) So right there, we're at or near our authorized headcount. In 2018, our actual head count was approximately 2,500 school crossing guards. That's approximately 340 more than we currently have today. In July 2023, our authorized headcount was reduced 18% from 2,702 to 2,219. That's approximately 483 fewer crossing guards. Every borough is reporting vacancies except Patrol Borough Queens South. Patrol Boroughs with significant vacancies are in Patrol Borough Manhattan North with 50 vacancies; Patrol Borough Brooklyn South has 36 vacancies; and Patrol Borough Manhattan South has 34 vacancies.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 101 Committee on Public Safety Other boroughs with vacancies or patrols are the Bronx with 14, Brooklyn North with nine, Queens North with seven, and Staten Island with seven. Commands with significant vacancies are the 2-3 Precinct in Manhattan North with 10; the 2-8 Precinct with 10 vacancies; and the 19th Precinct with seven. That's the overall picture when we talk about school crossing guards.

Okay. Do you feel there is a shortage of crossing guards? Because I served on the school board for four years, and in every meeting, I hear that crossing guards may come in the morning, and then they are assigned somewhere else in the afternoon. I'm still hearing it, because I still go to school board meetings. Is there a shortage of that? Can you talk about it?

So what I can say is, we currently publicly posted, we have 2,639 posts publicly posted. So that means that we have authorized these posts in the past, and they're not all being filled. But we are at or close to our

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 102 Committee on Public Safety authorized headcount. But the Office of Management and Budget would be able to better speak to that.

Again, from my perspective, what we do is, since we've been below budgeted headcount, we try to get up to budgeted headcount, and then we will work with OMB to increase our authorized headcount accordingly. So that's an ongoing situation. As we speak, we're 149 below, as the Chief had mentioned. So once we have this hire-back coming up in May, we'll be closer to the budgeted headcount and continue to work with OMB to adjust that allocation accordingly.
Is pay the problem of attracting people for the work or something else? Is outreach an issue? What is causing these vacancies? Let's start with crossing guards.

Right. So, crossing guard recruitment efforts are very similar to School Safety Agents. We utilize our Borough Coordinators, as well as our Level II Supervisors, to do their recruitment, as well as officers. And then we ask our partners in the DOE, our community partners, PTAs, to help in a recruitment process.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 103 Committee on Public Safety We also leverage social media to get the word out. But you know, school crossing guards are unique. They're local, they're working in close proximity, and they live in close proximity to the schools. They're often retirees, or they have children who are school age, so this is a position that works for their families. So we are, as the numbers show, and what I explained to you, we’re at or very close to our allotment, especially when you count in the 100 that are coming in for May 11th of 2026. Once we bring that 100 in, we're going to meet or be very close to our allotment.
Thank you.
Thank you so much. I'll save my next question for round two.
Perfect. Thank you so much.
Thank you. Council Member Ariola?

Thank you, Chair. So my questions may seem a little redundant, because I agree with Chair Feliz and Chair Dinowitz — I almost said Epstein, because that's where

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 104 Committee on Public Safety I was before I came here, Chair Dinowitz — is that your numbers are just not adding up, right? So, I would just want to go back to numbers. What is your vacancy? You said 360?
That's correct.
That's correct? So realistically with-- and how many are on staff, how many are working? How many agents do you have?
Right, 3,555.
Okay, 3,555. And then we have how many schools?
Roughly over 1,800 schools.
Okay, 1,800 schools. And the number of students that are in those schools goes into the tens of thousands, correct?
That is correct.

So there really is no possible way that you could be staffing with such a low headcount to the ratio of schools to students. There's no way for you to be staffing that. And yet you say you are staffing that, but you're staffing it with overtime being off the charts.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 105 Committee on Public Safety Now, you said there was a class of 1,000 that was--did I get that right? One thousand that have come through the class?
No, candidates. There are...
Candidates?
Yeah, for the Assistant School Safety Agent title, and then 881, who just passed the School Safety Agent test.
So they've passed- 881?
Yes.
Okay, so now, when will that list begin to be called?
I don't have that. I'm not privy to that information yet.
So they passed the test, they go on the list, and then you have to wait for OMB to fund it? Are there lines open for this? Obviously, 360 lines are open.

So just to clarify from the OMB perspective, we work with them to get approval to hire, and there's been no issue getting their approval to hire SSAs.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 106 Committee on Public Safety
So, what do you think a timeline is?
I think it goes back to when the list becomes certified, and then we have our Personnel Bureau have to vet the individual candidates and perform background checks.
How long does it take for a list to be certified?
I don't have the answer to that.
Does anyone know? Where did DOE go?
We can definitely get back to you on that.

Okay, so, as Chair Dinowitz said, if you have someone with your group that's here who could find those answers out, that's much better than telling us you don’t have the answer. I walked in here completely on your side, and I'm sitting here thinking, what's going on here? How many call-outs per day do you get from the agents that you have on? People get sick, and they don't come in. What happens at a school that

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 107 Committee on Public Safety has one Safety Agent and they're sick that day? What happens?
At all times, there will be a one School Safety Agent at every school in New York City.
Do you have floaters?

Yes, you would have floaters. That's why I keep bringing, uh, instituting administrative rollout and our mobile task force. I said at the beginning, well, actually I had to go back to it, but I had mentioned that we transferred over 100 agents that were assigned to administrative spots back to schools. As I said, we also have over 100 Assistant School Safety Agents assigned to elementary schools. Probably the numbers, and maybe I should have clarified that. I'm trying to ascertain what the number is, but most of the schools that we cover are elementary schools. That's probably why the number doesn't add up. So elementary schools, obviously, they're going to be a smaller size, you know, they're probably going to have 200-300 kids. And those are the schools that we're really, really pushing for,

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 108 Committee on Public Safety uh, for the title of Assistant School Safety Agent to take the title, so that we could send those to reinforce deployment at the schools where we might probably have a minimum of one School Safety... (CROSS-TALK)
The elementary schools go to what grade? Under your purview, what does it go to? Middle school? Does it go up to middle school?
Yes... (CROSS-TALK)
So, say from pre-K to 6th grade?
Yeah, 6th grade.
Sixth grade. So, when you have middle schools, you have to have more at the middle schools. You have to have more Safety Agents?
Yes, which we do...
At the middle schools, and you have to have the metal detectors at some or most of the middle schools... (CROSS-TALK)

At some of those. Metal detectors are mostly in high schools, and if it happens to-- obviously, some of the schools are co-

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 109 Committee on Public Safety located. So you might have a campus where (TIMER) it’s a high school but also has a junior high school.

Right, well, we have a lot of schools that are co-located, right? We have junior high schools and high schools. Chair, just a few more minutes? So what I'm trying to say is that what you're saying is not making sense. So if you have to take somebody from another school, a middle school that has metal detectors, and they have six Safety Guards — I have one in my district who has that — so you're going to pull from there, and then put them at-- is that what the mobile unit is? Pulling from one place and appointing them to another?
We do our best not to redeploy personnel who are assigned to scanning in schools, because we understand how that may have an impact on the operational needs of the school.
Any idea how many schools on any given day do not have any SSA Officers?

Zero. At all times, you can walk into any New York City public school,

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 110 Committee on Public Safety and there will be a minimum of one School Safety Agent. And when I say one School Safety Agent, that will probably be an elementary school. Every other school will definitely have more than that.
Okay, and if it's a middle school and they have at least one, and there's a lot going...
More. More...

As Chair Dinowitz said, watching the cameras, watching the metal detector, if they have one, walking through the hallways, if there is an altercation. That's just one person, right? So what we're hearing is that we're not getting people on the job fast enough. We need to get these 360 lines filled. We need to get people to come in. But I'm also hearing that they're not being deployed properly, either. How many are out on long-term sick? How many do you have out on long-term sick?
Just give me one second to get that information for you — 119.

Okay, 119. I cannot imagine that you have, with that much of a headcount, the proper staffing to keep the

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 111 Committee on Public Safety schools and the children in those schools safe. And I can't imagine that you're not pulling, even if it's from a public school that has K-5, you're not pulling a Safety Agent from there. I know for a fact that some of those Safety Agents are pulled from the grammar schools in our districts, and then there's no one. And then what happens is a PTA mom sits there, or the Parent Coordinator sits there. So what you're testifying to, and what we're seeing in actuality, does not match. So I think that you're kind of digging a bit of a hole for yourself for what you don't know, the testimony that you're giving, saying that we have stats that debunk your facts, and the fact that OMB is holding up on 881 people, who are certified, and could get out there. I'm happy to hear, though, that in Queensborough South, we do have a good number of guards, because that's where I'm from.
Thank you.
One...

This is why we have to have these hearings, and thank you, both

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 112 Committee on Public Safety Chairs, for doing this. Because we have to keep the children safe, and we have to keep the people who are working in the school safe. And we just don't seem to have the number of people necessary to do that. This is my final question. Do you blame that on what the salary is for your title?
I can’t speak on that because salary negotiations are the purview of the NYPD. I mean, do I believe that every City employee deserves better pay? Absolutely.
What's the incoming salary for a Safety Agent?

Okay, $40,480. All right, well, hopefully you do get back to the Chairs with the answers for the questions that you didn't have answers to, and hopefully we can get more Safety Agents on. OMB's got to get moving. We’ve got to start pulling. And DOE put some pressure — put some pressure. These are your schools — these are your schools.
Thank you.

May I just add? So we are working with OMB to get another class. I think the

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 113 Committee on Public Safety next class we're looking to do is around May for approximately 100 school Safety Agents. I know we always want a bigger number, but 100, I think, is what we'll realistically be able to pull in out of that 800. As I said, there's a timeframe here, and our goal is to hire as many as we can.
Thank you, thank you so much.
Thank you.
Thank you. Thanks for the extra time.

Thank you, thank you so much. And also I agree 100% with Council Member Ariola, that based on the information that all of you are stating today, including students being made late to class due to the fact that the scanning equipment is breaking down on a daily basis; 20% of the people calling out on a daily or weekly basis, I think it's very, very, very clear that the School Safety Division has a lot of needs. And I just wish that the NYPD would be a little bit clearer on that, rather than us having to just pull the information out of you.

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 114 Committee on Public Safety If you have needs, this is why we have these budget hearings. And I just wish that all of you would be a little bit clearer on your needs, so that we could resolve the issues that have existed for far too long, and that are having real negative consequences in our school communities.

For clarification, we have never negated the fact that we have vacancies, as I stated before. But that still, and I remain, and I stand tall on that, that hasn't deviated from School Safety keeping schools safe.
Right, yes.
Thank you.

You've never negated that--you've never said anything contrary to that. It's clear that there are issues related to headcount, budget issues, and also equipment issues. I just wish that all of you would be a little bit clearer on those needs, rather than us having to discover them through questioning. If there's issues with the NYPD School Safety Division, this is what we have budget hearings for. So that we can learn about the issues, and we could hopefully fund them, so that next year the

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 115 Committee on Public Safety issue won't exist. And it just sucks that we have to pull the information out of you rather than all of you just giving us the needs that you have.
I want to point out that the class of 100, that’s for some of the 360 vacancies, right?
Correct.

Okay, so the 360 vacancies still don't get you up to the 5,000 we had pre-pandemic. But I want to ask the DOE. As I said in my opening statement, because there aren't enough School Safety Agents, and because, despite what they testified to, there's forced overtime resulting in a lot of comp time, and they get a lot of days off, which they've earned, 20% absent rate, I think you testified to. There are principals who are forced to work with their UFT reps to create comp time positions — Comp time positions to patrol the halls, comp time positions to work in the lunchroom, jobs that would otherwise typically be done by School Safety Agents. Are you aware of this issue that is going on in some of our schools?

I'm not aware of any comp time positions that have to be created by

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 116 Committee on Public Safety teachers or for teachers to do hall patrols and so forth. There is something in the system, as you know, in the contract that allows, through Circular 6, for these assignments to be assigned to teachers, but I don't know of any comp time positions, unless it is before the contractual day or after the contractual day.
Before the contractual...
Start of the school (INAUDIBLE)... (CROSS-TALK)
Oh, start of school day, well...
(INAUDIBLE) staff member.
All right, well, the comp time positions are taking teachers out of the classroom to do other duties, administrative duties.

I don't know of any cases where that is happening. I don't dispute whether or not it is happening in a school where, in fact, there may be a shortfall of School Safety Agents. I do reiterate that the importance of safety

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 117 Committee on Public Safety is the responsibility of all adults in the building. Uh... (CROSS-TALK)

Agree, but I'm talking simply from a fiscal perspective that a teacher's salary can be over six figures, over $100,000. That's significantly more expensive for a system than $40,000-$50,000 for School Safety Agents. So, just simply from a budgetary perspective, it seems like we as a city are spending money-- instead of spending money on teachers doing comp time positions, or hiring an extra dean for a teacher, instead of hiring a teacher. It seems to me that it's not the wisest use of our funds. But it seems that the DOE doesn't collect data, or even anecdotal or qualitative data, on why these comp time positions are being created or why principals feel the need to hire extra deans outside of what they would have otherwise hired.
For the purposes of safety, I'm not aware of any data collected for those purposes.

I understand that– - Remind me what they're called, the School Safety Agents that are 18, 19, 20 years old?

The Committee on Education, Jointly with the 118 Committee on Public Safety
Assistant.
Assistant, thank you. The Assistant School Safety Agents were created because school aides were doing so much of that work that it was a new position that you created. Is that accurate?
Yes, it was created with the intent to create career opportunities for young adults, and obviously to create a clearer path to the title of School Safety Agents as well.
And to also clarify that school aides shouldn't be the ones sitting at desks, unless absolutely necessary, but there was so much of that going on that you created these positions?
That's the reason why we continue to push... (CROSS-TALK)
